```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This vignette evaluates genome-based predictions on real, public data:
*Klebsiella pneumoniae* isolates from NCBI Pathogen Detection with laboratory
susceptibility results for meropenem and ciprofloxacin. The predictions come
from simple rules applied to AMRFinderPlus genotypes, two per antimicrobial
(see `?amr_example_data`). The rules are illustrative; the point is the
evaluation.

```{r setup}
library(AMRvalid)
d <- amr_example_data()
x <- amr_import_predictions(d)
x
```

## Step 1: what is in the data?

```{r summary}
s <- amr_data_summary(x)
s[, c("model_id", "drug_name", "n_isolates", "n_S", "n_I_SDD", "n_R", "prevalence_R")]
```

Isolates come from `r length(unique(d$bioproject))` studies (BioProjects).
Many are relatives: `r sum(!is.na(unique(d[, c("isolate_id", "genomic_cluster")])$genomic_cluster))`
isolates fall into `r length(unique(na.omit(d$genomic_cluster)))` NCBI SNP
clusters, and the largest cluster holds
`r max(table(unique(d[, c("isolate_id", "genomic_cluster")])$genomic_cluster))`
isolates. That structure matters below.

```{r validate}
amr_validate(x)
```

The reference contains intermediate (I) results. The rules only predict S
or R, so I is handled explicitly: binary metrics exclude it (the default),
and the AST agreement metrics count it as a minor error.

## Step 2: performance per predictor

```{r eval}
e <- amr_evaluate(x)
key <- c("sensitivity", "specificity", "categorical_agreement",
         "very_major_error", "major_error", "minor_error")
tab <- as.data.frame(e)[e$metric %in% key, c("drug_name", "model_id", "metric", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
tab[, c("estimate", "lower", "upper")] <- round(tab[, c("estimate", "lower", "upper")], 3)
rownames(tab) <- NULL
tab
```

The broader rule for each antimicrobial trades very major errors (resistant
isolates called susceptible) for major errors (susceptible isolates called
resistant).

## Step 3: do outbreak clones flatter the results?

Public collections over-represent outbreaks. Weighting each SNP cluster
equally (isolates outside a cluster count as their own group) shows how the
rules perform across distinct strains rather than across isolates.

```{r weighting}
k <- c("sensitivity", "specificity", "very_major_error", "major_error")
iso <- as.data.frame(amr_evaluate(x))
clu <- as.data.frame(amr_evaluate(x, weight_by = "genomic_cluster"))
cmp <- merge(iso[iso$metric %in% k, c("model_id", "metric", "estimate")],
             clu[clu$metric %in% k, c("model_id", "metric", "estimate")],
             by = c("model_id", "metric"), suffixes = c("_isolates", "_clusters"))
cmp$change <- cmp$estimate_clusters - cmp$estimate_isolates
cmp[, 3:5] <- round(cmp[, 3:5], 3)
cmp <- cmp[order(cmp$metric, cmp$model_id), ]
rownames(cmp) <- NULL
cmp
```

The very major error rate is higher for all four rules once each cluster
counts once, and QRDR-only sensitivity falls from 0.79 to 0.72: well-predicted
outbreak clones make the isolate-level numbers look better than performance
across distinct strains.

## Step 4: intervals that respect clustering

```{r bootstrap}
mero <- x[x$drug == "MEM", ]
b_iso <- amr_bootstrap(mero, group = "isolate_id", B = 300, seed = 1)
b_clu <- amr_bootstrap(mero, group = "genomic_cluster", B = 300, seed = 1)
vme <- function(b, unit) {
  b <- as.data.frame(b)
  r <- b[b$metric == "very_major_error", ]
  data.frame(model = r$model_id, resampled = unit, groups = r$n_groups,
             estimate = round(r$estimate, 3), lower = round(r$lower, 3), upper = round(r$upper, 3))
}
rbind(vme(b_iso, "isolates"), vme(b_clu, "SNP clusters"))
```

Resampling clusters rather than isolates widens the intervals, because the
`r b_iso$n_groups[1]` isolates carry the information of only
`r b_clu$n_groups[1]` independent groups.

## Step 5: comparing the two meropenem rules on the same isolates

```{r paired}
amr_paired_compare(mero, models = c("carbapenemase genes", "carbapenemase or porin + ESBL/AmpC"),
                   group = "genomic_cluster", B = 300, seed = 1)
```

The broader rule lowers the very major error rate and raises the major error
rate by a similar amount, leaving overall accuracy unchanged. Which rule is
preferable depends on which error matters more in practice.

## Step 6: stability over time

```{r time}
x$period <- cut(d$collection_year, c(-Inf, 2016, 2020, Inf), labels = c("up to 2016", "2017-2020", "2021 on"))
per <- lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(x)), x$period), function(i) {
  r <- as.data.frame(amr_evaluate(x[i, ], validate = FALSE))
  r <- r[r$metric %in% c("n", "very_major_error"), c("model_id", "metric", "estimate")]
  r
})
per <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(p, nm) cbind(period = nm, p), per, names(per)))
w <- reshape(per, idvar = c("period", "model_id"), timevar = "metric", direction = "wide")
names(w) <- sub("estimate.", "", names(w))
w$very_major_error <- round(w$very_major_error, 3)
w$period <- factor(w$period, levels = levels(x$period))
w <- w[order(w$model_id, w$period), ]
rownames(w) <- NULL
w
```

Isolates without a collection year are left out of this table. The QRDR-only
rule misses far more resistant isolates collected from 2021 on, while the rule
that also counts plasmid-mediated quinolone resistance genes stays accurate.
Changes over time can reflect new resistance mechanisms, changing breakpoints
or different submitting studies; the table shows that performance is not
stable, not why.

## Step 7: a report for the paper

```{r report}
dataset_info <- list(source = "NCBI Pathogen Detection PDG000000012.2568",
                     breakpoint_standard = "As submitted to BioSample (not recorded)")
model_info <- list(description = "Rule-based interpretation of AMRFinderPlus calls",
                   training_data = "None (rules, not trained models)",
                   threshold_selection = "Not applicable (binary rules)")
report <- amr_report(x, e, b_clu, dataset_info = dataset_info, model_info = model_info,
                     file = file.path(tempdir(), "ncbi-report.md"))
p <- amr_provenance(x, e, b_clu, dataset_info = dataset_info, model_info = model_info)
table(p$status)
p[p$status == "not assessable", c("tripod_item", "item")]
```

The report lists every TRIPOD+AI item it covers and flags the ones still
missing. The list above is the author's to-do list before submission.

## Caveats

* Phenotypes were interpreted by the submitting laboratories under breakpoints
  that are not recorded, and may differ between studies.
* The isolates are those with submitted antibiograms, not a random sample.
* The rules have no training data, so no split checks apply here; for trained
  models, start with `amr_validate_splits()` (see the vignette on
  population-aware evaluation).
